transcript.text: bosch washer FD 9409 not draining. ive cleaned the filter already. what part do i need?

FD 9409 dates the washer to September 2014, but it does not identify the exact pump. Bosch parts must be matched using the full E-Nr model number (for example `WAN…/01` or `WAE…GB/xx`) from the sticker inside the door opening or on the rear.

If the filter is clear, the usual possibilities are:

1. Drain pump blocked or failed — most likely part, but inspect first.
• Unplug the washer.
• Remove the filter and check whether the pump impeller behind it turns with slight magnetic “steps.”
• Remove any debris such as a bra wire, coin, hairpin, fabric, etc.
• If it only hums, has no movement, leaks, or measures electrically open, it likely needs a drain pump.

2. Drain hose / sink trap blockage
• Disconnect the drain hose from the plumbing and check it is not kinked or blocked.
• Try draining into a bucket. If it drains then, the washer pump is probably fine and the household waste pipe is blocked.

3. Internal sump-to-pump hose blockage
• Small items can be trapped in the large rubber hose between tub and pump. This requires removing a lower/rear panel and is messier.

Do not order a pump based only on “Bosch FD 9409”: several different pumps were used. Send the full E-Nr and /xx index, plus any displayed error code (often E:18 for drainage), and I can tell you the correct part number.
E-Nr bit of the sticker is rubbed off so I can't read it. Display shows E18. Impeller turns but feels a bit stiff and gritty, pump just hums, and the drain hose is clear. So is it the pump I need?

Yes — based on E18, a clear drain hose/filter, and a pump that hums but will not turn properly, the drain pump is the most likely failed part.

The gritty/stiff feel strongly suggests either:

• debris lodged behind/around the impeller, or
• a worn/seized pump rotor/bearing.

Before ordering, it is worth checking for a hidden obstruction because it can mimic a failed pump:

1. Unplug the machine and drain remaining water.
2. Remove the filter.
3. Shine a torch into the pump cavity and try turning the impeller.
• It should turn with a slightly notchy magnetic resistance, but not feel sandy, scrape, or bind.
4. If possible, remove the pump from underneath/front access and inspect its inlet and the large tub-to-pump hose for items such as a bra wire, coin, hair grip, etc.

If it still hums and is gritty/stiff with nothing trapped, replace the complete drain pump assembly/motor (not just the filter cap).

Because the E-Nr is unreadable, do not buy a pump solely from the FD number. Remove the existing pump and use the number moulded/printed on it. Common Bosch pumps may be made by Askoll, Copreci, or Plaset and have their own model/part number; match:

• electrical rating/voltage (normally 220–240 V),
• connector type,
• mounting arrangement (usually twist-lock or screws),
• hose outlet orientation, and
• part number on the old pump.

A clear photo of the old pump label, connector, and mounting would let a parts supplier identify it.
